site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Loyal Hearts, A Deer Set Free
stories.source: Rohantamiga Jataka, The Jataka, vol. IV, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: In a forest glade, Rohanta, the splendid leader of a great deer herd, found his hoof caught tight in a hunter's snare. Far from panicking, the Bodhisatta deer stayed calm, his great antlers still and his breath steady beneath the woven cords.

His brother Chittamiga rushed forward to distract the hunter, while his gentle sister Sutana spoke softly for Rohanta's release. So struck were they all by the deer's loyal family and quiet wisdom that the hunter loosened the snare and set him free.

Then Rohanta taught the hunter the gentle way of compassion, and the man listened, releasing his heart as well as the deer. Together Rohanta, Chittamiga, and Sutana bounded back to their herd, their loyalty turning a snare into lasting friendship.

stories.title: Rama Guards the Sacred Fire
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Bala Kanda (Gita Press translation)
body: When sage Vishvamitra sought help for his sacred sacrifice, troubled again and again by demons, he turned to King Dasharatha of Ayodhya. The king, though heavy-hearted, entrusted his young sons Rama and Lakshmana to the sage's care, trusting that obedience would shield them on the forest path.

Vishvamitra taught the brothers the divine disciplines that steady the mind, then led them through the woods to the sacrificial grounds. There Rama struck down the fierce demoness Tataka and, when Maricha and Subahu fell upon the rite, drove them away so the holy offerings could burn undisturbed.

With the fire tended and the demons scattered, the sages rejoiced as the yajna was completed whole. Young Rama had offered his courage as service, standing guard so a community's prayer could rise, a quiet promise of protection fulfilled.

stories.title: The Bridge of the Monkey King
stories.source: Mahakapi Jataka, The Jataka, vol. V, H. T. Francis translation (public domain)
body: Along a river beside a mango grove, the Bodhisatta ruled a troop of monkeys. When King Brahmadatta's men came to capture them, the monkey king stretched himself between a tree and the far bank, becoming a living bridge so his followers could cross to safety.

One by one the monkeys fled across his trembling body while the human king watched in wonder. Brahmadatta then ordered the injured Bodhisatta gently lifted down, and the monkey king quietly taught him what true leadership meant: a ruler's joy is found in protecting those who depend on him.
Touched by such selfless bravery, King Brahmadatta honored the Bodhisatta and carried the lesson home. Compassionate leadership, he learned, is the strongest kingdom of all.

stories.title: A Deer Steps Forward in Love
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: In a king's park, two herds of deer lived beneath daily threat, each day one chosen for the royal table. To spare their kin the endless hunt, the deer took turns among themselves, sharing the burden gently.

When a pregnant doe's turn fell, she asked the noble Banyan Deer, leader of her herd, for a little more time until her fawn could be born. Without hesitation, he stepped forward and laid himself upon the block in her place.

The king, watching this quiet act of selflessness, felt his heart soften. He freed the Banyan Deer, then the doe, and at last every creature in the park, so the deer might live safe beneath his care, guarded by the love their sacrifice had awakened.

stories.title: The Rabbit Who Heard the Palm
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: Under a tall palm tree, a small rabbit dozed until a ripe fruit dropped with a sudden thump. Convinced the earth was cracking open beneath him, he bolted through the forest, his heart racing with imagined doom.

One by one, other rabbits, deer, and great beasts joined the frightened stampede toward the sea, none of them pausing to ask why. At the water's edge, a wise lion raised his paw and asked gently for the rabbit to show him the danger.

Together they walked back to the palm tree, where the fruit lay whole and still on the ground. The lion smiled, the rabbit sighed with relief, and every creature turned homeward, the forest at peace again because someone had checked the truth.
